stories.title: The Tortoise and the Hare
stories.author: Aesop
stories.blurb: Slow and steady can win the race.
stories.imageAlt: A tortoise and a hare racing, illustration by Milo Winter
stories.moral: Slow and steady wins the race.
paragraphs: A Hare liked to tease a Tortoise for being so slow.
“I am the fastest!” said the Hare. “You could never beat me.”
“Shall we race?” asked the Tortoise.
The Hare laughed, but he said yes. They lined up, and the race began.
The Hare ran far ahead. Then he lay down for a nap. “The Tortoise is so slow,” he thought. “I have plenty of time.”
The Tortoise kept walking, step by step. He did not stop.
When the Hare woke up, he ran as fast as he could. But the Tortoise had already crossed the finish line.
The Tortoise had won!

stories.title: The Lion and the Mouse
stories.author: Aesop
stories.blurb: A tiny friend can help a big one.
stories.imageAlt: A lion and a mouse, illustration by Milo Winter
stories.moral: Little friends may prove great friends.
paragraphs: One day a Lion was sleeping in the sun. A little Mouse ran across his nose.
The Lion woke up and caught the Mouse with his big paw.
“Please let me go!” cried the Mouse. “Someday I may help you.”
The Lion laughed. How could a tiny Mouse help a Lion? But he let the Mouse go.
Later, hunters caught the Lion in a strong net. He could not get free.
The little Mouse heard the Lion roar. She ran to help.
She chewed and chewed on the ropes until the Lion was free.
“Thank you, little friend,” said the Lion. “You were right!”

stories.title: The Fox and the Grapes
stories.author: Aesop
stories.blurb: What we cannot reach may seem sour.
stories.imageAlt: A fox looking up at grapes, illustration by Milo Winter
stories.moral: It is easy to hate what you cannot get.
paragraphs: A hungry Fox saw some sweet grapes hanging high on a vine.
“Those grapes look perfect,” said the Fox. “I will get some.”
He jumped and jumped, but the grapes were too high.
He tried again and again. Still he could not reach them.
At last the Fox walked away. “Those grapes are probably sour,” he said.
But really, he only said that because he could not have them.

stories.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
stories.author: Aesop
stories.blurb: Work today to be ready for tomorrow.
stories.imageAlt: An ant and a grasshopper, illustration by Milo Winter
stories.moral: It is best to prepare for the days of need.
paragraphs: All summer, an Ant worked hard. She carried food to her nest.
A Grasshopper sang and played in the warm sun.
“Why work so hard?” asked the Grasshopper. “Come and sing with me!”
“I am storing food for winter,” said the Ant. “You should do the same.”
But the Grasshopper only laughed and kept on singing.
When winter came, the ground was cold and bare. The Grasshopper had nothing to eat.
He went to the Ant. “Please share your food,” he said.
The Ant had worked all summer, so she had food. The Grasshopper wished he had worked too.

stories.title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
stories.author: Aesop
stories.blurb: People stop listening when we tell fibs.
stories.imageAlt: A shepherd boy calling for help, illustration by Milo Winter
stories.moral: Liars are not believed even when they speak the truth.
paragraphs: A Shepherd Boy watched sheep near a dark forest. He felt bored.
To amuse himself, he ran toward the village and shouted, “Wolf! Wolf!”
The villagers came running to help. But there was no wolf. The boy laughed.
A few days later, he did it again. “Wolf! Wolf!” The villagers ran to help, and again he laughed.
Then one evening, a real wolf came out of the forest!
The boy shouted, “Wolf! Wolf!” But this time the villagers did not come.
“He cannot fool us again,” they said.
The wolf scared the sheep, and the boy learned a hard lesson: if you tell fibs, people may not believe you when you tell the truth.
